_note: TOP 8. Each list is released whole; the newest `released` is on show and the rest are at /top8/archive/. Each entry: what it is, why it made the list, and which law of the seven it trips, at `rank` on its list. 'mine' points at a work on the shelf when the work is a genuine source for that entry - not an advert, the citation.

lists.title: Top 8 parasocial moments in Saturday morning cartoons of the 1990s
lists.home_hook: Every one of these is a one-sided relationship with a person who does not exist, aimed at a child, on a Saturday, before anybody had a word for it.
lists.dek: Every one of these is a one-sided relationship with a person who does not exist, aimed at a child, on a Saturday, before anybody had a word for it. Ranked by how well it worked.
lists.standfirst: This is the section nobody argues about, because it started before anyone had an argument. A child watching a cartoon is doing the same thing a forty-year-old watching a stream is doing, and the only difference is that nobody had decided yet whether it counted.
lists.frame_note:
There is not one frame of the shows themselves anywhere on this list. Whatever studio made each character, none of it is free to reuse, so wherever there is a photograph at all it is of **the audience**, and of the life the shows had outside the screen: a roller coaster, a party, a costume, a panel at a convention.

{blank} of the {total} have no photograph at all, so their entries carry no picture. The absence is part of the record: every entry here is a relationship with a character who cannot answer, and a relationship like that leaves the evidence on one side only - ours.

entries.name: The letter from the NEST
entries.what: Tommy writes to a magazine telling them the NEST was real. The NEST never appears. The letter is never answered. Chuckie and Tommy argue about it and then forget about it and then the episode ends.
entries.why: The single most parasocial thing ever put on television, and it is a joke about wanting the writers to confirm that a fictional place is real. An eight-year-old asking to be told the world is real, dressed up as a joke about a brand of baby food. Everything on this site happens because a child did not accept the terms of the arrangement.

entries.name: The client in the basement
entries.what: Sherman Grant is twelve and has a junior detective kit. When Batman is hit with nerve gas and collapses into the Batmobile, Sherman and Roberta drive him home, lay him on a couch in the basement, and set up a crime lab around him. Roberta wants to call the police. Sherman refuses: a detective has to protect the identity of his client, especially when it is this client. The Penguin comes to the house. The kids hold him off with the contents of Batman's utility belt until Batman wakes up.
entries.why: The relationship is entirely Sherman's invention. Batman cannot consent, cannot answer, and spends most of the episode unconscious; the child supplies the client, the duty, and the confidentiality. This is the list's arrangement at its most literal: the hero is in the room, and the child builds a professional ethics around a body that cannot say yes. The audience is doing the same thing from the couch. Batman wakes up, solves the plot, and leaves; the boy keeps the story.

entries.name: Will you help me?
entries.what: The host asks the child at home a question, straight into the camera, and then waits through a silence written into the script before behaving as though an answer arrived. The pause is not dead air. The show was built out of it.
entries.why: A 1997 New York Times piece recorded a mother muddled that her small son had begun answering the television, and the period's research found children engaging more the more they rewatched. The show aimed second-person grammar at children young enough not to know a machine was doing it, and the question it put in the pause was four words long: 'Will you help me?' That is the whole transaction - attachment made by a gap left open long enough for a three-year-old to step into it.

entries.name: Tommy finds the gun and it works
entries.what: The premise of the entire show, which is four toddlers exploring a house while believing they are the size of insects. And they are. The house is as big as a city to them.
entries.why: Rugrats is a parasocial engine pointed at children who could not yet identify the trick. The scale is the relationship: the world is enormous, you are small, and there is always one adult-shaped thing that will explain it. That is the whole emotional structure of the show and most people still have it.

entries.name: The player at the keyboard
entries.show: Where on Earth Is Carmen Sandiego?, 1994
entries.what: The show opened and closed on a live-action kid at a computer, seen from behind, playing a Carmen Sandiego game. The cartoon was the game. Carmen talked to the player - not to Zack and Ivy, but to the person at the keyboard - and the player sent the detectives to the next location. The show never showed the player's face, because the face was yours.
entries.why: The frame is a machine for making the viewer complicit. The child at home is not watching a cartoon about detectives; the child is the player, and Carmen is the voice coming out of the game. The live-action back of a head is the only body the show gives you, and it is enough. Every episode ends with the player still at the keyboard and Carmen still out there, which is the exact shape of the relationship.

entries.name: The moral delivered by the character
entries.what: At the end of every dubbed episode the Scouts stepped out of the story and spoke to the viewer directly - thirty seconds about friendship, homework or courage, tied to whatever the episode had just done, in new lines recorded over the existing footage. The person who had just saved the world stayed behind to talk to you.
entries.why: It was not an artistic flourish: the segment was added to the English dub to satisfy the educational-content requirements of the Children's Television Act. The machinery of children's television produced a character looking straight at a child and giving advice, in character, because a law asked for teaching - and the thing it taught with was the bond itself, which needed no writing at all.

entries.name: The grouch on the telethon
entries.what: Oscar the Grouch refused to perform in a fundraiser telethon and was written out of the special for a season. He came back. Millions of children wrote in about it.
entries.why: The cleanest case in television of a fictional character having genuine leverage over the people who own him. Sesame Street is parasocial infrastructure - a generation of people grew up with these characters and still argues about them as if they are relatives - and the grouch episode is that infrastructure noticing it had power.

entries.name: The User outside the Net
entries.what: ReBoot was set inside a computer. The city of Mainframe was full of sprites and binomes who knew that their world was run by a being called the User, who lived outside the Net and dropped games on them for pleasure. The User never appeared. The User was the person at the computer, which is to say the viewer. The opening narration said no one knew for sure what the User wanted, but Bob intended to find out.
entries.why: The show made the audience the absent god of a whole civilization. The sprites fear the User's games and argue about whether the User is one being or many; the User is never in the room, and the User is the child on the couch. It is the most literal version of the list's arrangement: a world of characters who exist only while you are watching, and a relationship you cannot reciprocate because you are the one holding the controller.

entries.name: The answer waited until after the break
entries.what: Before the commercial break the show put one of its creatures on screen as a silhouette and asked the audience to name it. The answer came after the adverts. Children shouted at the television anyway, because the question was addressed to them and the pause was real.
entries.why: The withholding is the design. The show borrows the child's knowledge against the clock, and the screen is a surface that cannot hear - which is this list's whole arrangement, delivered in the gap between two adverts. The shouting is the audience enthusiastically holding up its end of a conversation the other side never scheduled.

entries.name: Hey Arnold, said to a room where nobody is Arnold
entries.what: A greet-the-world catchphrase, delivered out loud, several times an episode, to rooms full of people who are not the person it is addressed to. It is a hello with no possibility of an answer, and it is the premise of the show rather than a joke inside it.
entries.why: It is the purest arrangement of the thing this whole site is about, and it is aimed at a child. Every other entry here has someone on one side of the relationship; this one has a child offering something to a room. Nobody ever responds, nothing is even meant to, and the greeting keeps being delivered anyway - which is not a parody of parasocial attachment, it is a working description of it, written for six-year-olds and never once signalled.

entries.name: The producer takes your call
entries.what: The show ended most episodes with a segment called Producer Says. The producer, voiced by Malcolm-Jamal Warner, answered a ringing phone and took a call from a viewer who had just watched the episode. The viewer pointed out what the cartoon got wrong: the volcano took thousands of years, the class could not have survived that, the bus could not do that. The producer agreed, blamed the half-hour slot, and thanked them for watching closely. Then the next episode did it again.
entries.why: The show built a reply into its own format. The viewer is not asked to write in and wait; the phone rings before the credits, and the show's own producer concedes the fiction's errors to a child's voice. It is a rare case of a children's show treating the audience as a fact-checker and a participant at the same time. The concession is the relationship: the show says it knows you were watching closely, and it would rather admit the lie than lose you.

entries.name: The hedgehog told you how to cross the street
entries.what: A short segment closed every episode: Sonic and Tails turn out of the fiction and give the child watching a piece of advice - seatbelts, smoking, sexual harassment - in character, straight at the viewer. The rescue ends and the character instructs.
entries.why: It was added under the Children's Television Act's educational rules, which is the honest frame: a law asked children's television to teach something, and what got built was the character you already loved, addressing you in second person at the end of the show. The educational content was the relationship, formalised.

entries.name: The dragon that waited
entries.what: Emperor Kukulkan is a fictional dragon who can only be summoned by a child who believes in him. Every child who believed in him could summon him.
entries.why: The premise is a description of parasocial attachment stated as a children's cartoon premise, and nobody at the time clocked it as one. Believing in something fictional is the mechanism. The show built an entire children's programme on it and treated it as unremarkable, which is exactly why it worked.

entries.name: The hosts in the comic book
entries.what: KaBlam! was an anthology of short cartoons, and between the shorts it was a comic book. Henry and June lived in its pages, turned them to introduce the next cartoon, and treated the whole show as a publication you were holding. The announcer called it a place where cartoons and comics collide and introduced the two of them as your hosts. They were not characters in the shorts. They were the frame, and the frame had a personality.
entries.why: The anthology had no continuing story, so the relationship was the frame: two voices who were always there between the cartoons, in a book you were holding. Henry and June were not your friends; they were the printed hosts of a printed object, and the show made no distinction between reading and watching. The bond was with the binding. That is a strange thing for a television show to ask a child to do, and KaBlam! asked it every week.

entries.name: The power is yours
entries.what: A hero who exists only when five children combine their rings and summon him - and at the end of the episode he turns to the audience, hands the power over and leaves. 'The power is yours!' is his farewell line.
entries.why: The fiction redistributes itself to the viewer as its final act. Every other entry here asks a child to believe in something; this one ends by telling the child the belief was the power all along, which is parasocial attachment stated as environmental policy and repeated weekly until it became a catchphrase.

entries.name: Mighty Morphin, you are the ranger
entries.what: Five teenagers in spandex, and the entire premise is that a group of people with no special qualities are chosen by a machine to fight monsters. Then the actors leave and new teenagers take the costumes and the audience carries over completely.
entries.why: The parasocial breach in full public view. Millions of children watched actors be replaced and transferred every piece of feeling they had for the character straight to whoever put the suit on. It was the most visible handover of an attachment ever broadcast, running five days a week, and it is the closest thing television has to a controlled experiment.

entries.name: The popsicle stick who read your mail
entries.what: Between cartoons on summer afternoons, Nickelodeon ran a block hosted by a popsicle stick. Stick Stickly had googly eyes, a jelly bean nose, and a PO box. He read viewer mail on the air, interviewed children, and sang his address so you could write to him: PO Box 963, New York City, New York State, 10108. In U-Dip, viewers voted on which substance to dip him in. In U-Pick, viewers voted on which cartoon to show.
entries.why: The host was a craft project with a face, and the host's whole job was the viewer's letter. He gave out a real PO box, sang it as a jingle, and made the address a thing children memorized. The relationship was not with a character in a story; it was with a stick who promised that if you wrote, he would read it. The stick was the reply.

entries.name: The turtles left the screen and played the concert
entries.what: In the fall of 1990 the four cartoon turtles went on a live arena tour, 'Coming Out of Their Shells' - a run of about forty cities that opened at Radio City Music Hall. Pizza Hut sponsored it, the opening night went out on pay-per-view, and the show's own spokesperson told a reporter: 'They are not actors dressed in costumes. They are the Ninja Turtles, and they've learned to play rock & roll.'
entries.why: The official position was that nobody was in a suit. Children watched four drawings walk onto a stage and the people behind the show stood behind the sentence that the drawings were the performers, because letting the costume be visible would have broken the only thing being sold. The characters moved in so completely that the staff had to deny the bodies underneath to keep them real.

entries.name: Doug's dad watching the TV in the dark
entries.what: Phil Funutmarsh sits in a dark room in front of the television and is, for a few seconds per episode, allowed to be a person who is merely a father.
entries.why: The show understood that the audience's relationship was not only with Doug. It built the person holding the remote into the fiction, gave him two lines a week, and let a generation of children feel oddly seen by a background character. The parasocial relationship with the dad is the one nobody has ever written about and it was aimed at children.

entries.name: The fan letter with a trap in it
entries.what: Buster and Babs open the viewer mail on screen. One letter is from a little girl in the hospital who says she is very sick and asks if Fifi La Fume can visit. Fifi cries and agrees to go. The girl is Elmyra Duff, whose running joke is wanting to keep Fifi as a pet; the letter was bait. The show stages the fan letter as a con and lets the character's sympathy be real.
entries.why: The letter is the whole arrangement in one envelope: a stranger claims a need, the character responds with real feeling, and the need turns out to be a trap. The show is not making fun of sick children. It is making fun of the viewer who has learned that a character will come if you write the right sentence. Fifi's tears are the far end's reply, and they are spent on a lie. The scary part is that the lie works because the character is exactly as kind as the fiction promised.

entries.name: Three new faces in the same suits
entries.what: In the fall of 1994, mid-series and five days a week, three of the five original rangers left the show and three new teenagers took the powers on screen in a ceremony. The audience watched everything attached to the old faces move to faces it had never seen, and kept watching.
entries.why: The most visible handover of an attachment ever broadcast. Millions of children transferred the feeling they had for Jason, Zack and Trini to Rocky, Adam and Aisha essentially on schedule, without being asked, and nobody pretended otherwise. Five days a week, in front of the same children, for years - which is the closest television has come to a controlled experiment on whether the attachment was ever to the person. It was to whoever was inside the suit.

entries.name: The rabbit in the hat
entries.what: A whole generation of children said a specific sentence in a specific order with a specific pause in it, for a cartoon rabbit, on Saturday morning.
entries.why: It is last because it is the least about plot and the most about the medium. The line was never written to be repeated. It was a delivery, and an entire cohort of children reproduced it, in unison, years later, without being asked. That is not attachment to a character. That is attachment to a voice, and it is the purest parasocial event in the list.

entries.name: The fan who had no life
entries.what: Fanboy is a teenager in a comic book store who decides that his life's purpose is to become Freakazoid's sidekick. Freakazoid, still mourning his last sidekick, does not want him. Fanboy follows him through an initiation, a fight, and a comic book convention. Freakazoid finally gets rid of him by introducing him to Mark Hamill, who is at the convention as himself. Fanboy is delighted. When Freakazoid asks if he really has no life, Fanboy says no, sir, proudly.
entries.why: The fan has learned the contract better than the hero: if you want the character to notice you, you have to get close enough to be a sidekick. The show answers with the thing the contract cannot survive - the hero says no, then hands the fan to a real person. Mark Hamill is the joke and the escape hatch: the fan wanted a fictional friend, and the show gives him a real celebrity who is at the convention as himself. The fan is happy anyway, which is the most honest part.

entries.name: The toy that laughed back
entries.what: A plush Elmo that giggled and shook when squeezed, sold for about twenty-five dollars in the Christmas season of 1996. Then it ran out: stores sold out as the trucks unloaded, resellers got hundreds for one doll, a Denver charity auction sold an Elmo for $10,000, and parents lined up by the hundreds for a shelf that was already empty.
entries.why: Here the character could be touched, and it responded to being touched. Every relationship on this site runs one way, and here was a plush object in the house that laughed when you reached for it - not an answer, but the shape of one, in the room. The frenzy was not about a toy. A character who had spent years talking to children from inside a screen could suddenly be held, and the supply could not cover the feeling.

lists.stage_doc: A list is released whole; the newest `released` date is the list on show and former lists move to /top8/archive/. Entries are `featured` when the list shipped with them or they were added to the pool afterwards, `candidate` while drafted for a future list.
lists.pool_note: `entries` is the pool: the list as released, in rank order, with later moments added among them, because the eight on show are a moving window over the whole pool. `released` orders the show/archive split; a list with no date sorts as the oldest.

lists.title: Top 8 parasocial moments when the reply was manufactured
lists.home_hook: Every reply on this list was manufactured on the near side; the far end is where it arrived from, not where it came from.
lists.dek: Every reply on this list was manufactured on the near side. The far end is where it arrived from, not where it came from.
lists.standfirst: Part one was cartoons, the version everyone agrees is harmless. This one is the machinery: the office that typed the reply, the card signed by a character, the meter that read the room, the tape that held the voice - and one entry where no reply ever came, from a girl who kept writing anyway. Ranked by how completely the reply was manufactured.

entries.name: A letter back from Carolyn Keene
entries.what: For fifty-four years young readers wrote to a detective who did not exist, and letters came back. The replies came from the Stratemeyer Syndicate's correspondence department under the house name Carolyn Keene, which was a slot in a production system rather than a person. The New York Public Library holds the letters themselves - boxes 56 and 57 - including a few written by parents on behalf of their children, and by adults who had read the books as kids.
entries.why: The reply was real, and it came from an office that had chosen not to have a face. Mildred Wirt Benson wrote 23 of the first 30 books and her identity was not made public until 1991, so almost every answer a child received arrived from a byline rather than a person. The tie as the reader lived it asked for nothing and was answered anyway - and the answering was manufactured, politely, for half a century.

entries.name: The paw that signed the fan mail
entries.what: Rin Tin Tin was found as a puppy in France in September 1918 and became a film star after Lee Duncan brought him to California. As his fame grew, fan letters arrived by the thousands, and the replies went out on a glossy portrait signed with an inked paw print above the words 'Most faithfully, Rin Tin Tin.'
entries.why: The paw was a signature the dog could not write. Somebody on the near side inked the print and sent the portrait, so the answer looked like an act of the animal rather than a piece of office work. The photograph was the reply, and the bond it answered was real.

entries.name: A reply from Beatrice Fairfax
entries.what: In 1898 three readers' letters asking for advice landed on the women's page of the Evening Journal, and the staff answered them under a name that did not exist: Beatrice Fairfax, after Dante's Beatrice and a family place in Virginia. Readers wrote to her personally - the mail reached up to 1,400 letters a day, and the Post Office eventually refused to deliver them, so the paper collected its own post. Marie Manning, a working journalist, wrote the replies, and the column ran, under her and then under others, for decades.
entries.why: The far end of this correspondence was a masthead. A stranger's most private letter was answered by a person, which is why it worked, and it came from a woman who had never been one, which is why the reply could be whatever the page needed it to be. Manning's own instruction to her readers was 'Dry your eyes, roll up your sleeves and dig for a practical solution' - advice the fictional Beatrice could give because she had no life of her own to protect. Every advice column since is the same machinery: a human being on the near side, and a signature on the far one that cannot be reached.

entries.name: Cordially yours, Betty Crocker
entries.what: In 1921 a flour company's mailroom was already answering letters of cooking questions when the advertising department asked for one name the answers could all sign. Betty Crocker answered for decades - letters first, a radio voice from 1924 - and every reply went out 'Cordially yours', in a real woman's handwriting, adopted from an employee's submission and still in use.
entries.why: The reply existed before the name did. The writers were real home economists; the name was created so the answers could come from somebody, and the company's own account of the effect is that the voice was 'like the woman next door dropping in'. What the reader attached to was Betty, and Betty was a signature. The labour was real, the relationship ran one way by design, and the correspondence continued under a single invented name for exactly that reason.

entries.name: The code was printed in the comic you were holding
entries.what: A reader sent in a code printed inside the comic they were holding and received a membership card, a certificate and a plastic Captain Marvel ring - issued under “the actual authority of Benj J. Grimm, Grand Marshal.”
entries.why: The bond was assembled by the person who was attached. Nobody built a private channel; the near side performed the decoding out of materials the far side printed, and the reply was signed by a character so it would read as coming from inside the story.

entries.name: The three secretaries who answered as Clara Bow
entries.what: In April 1928 Clara Bow received 33,727 items of fan mail in a single month, more than a thousand a day. Three full-time secretaries answered it on her behalf.
entries.why: The reader wrote to a star and the answer came from an office of three. The labour was real; the voice was a small staff. A reply that looked like one woman's attention was manufactured at industrial scale, and the scale is what made the attention believable.

entries.name: The post office wrote back as Santa
entries.what: Letters addressed to Santa Claus were, by rule, unmailable, because the address was fictitious; the Dead Letter Office opened them, returned what it could, and destroyed the rest. Postal clerks broke the rule quietly for years - in the mid-1890s the clerks in Washington let a 'rich old man' take a few dozen letters and fulfil them 'as coming from their patron saint', and in 1894 a Connecticut postmaster named Harris Eames opened a letter to 'Sandy Clous' from a girl he knew and organised the town's businesses into a Christmas for her. Permission was given, revoked and given again until 1912, when Postmaster General Frank Hitchcock made answering official: in most offices the reply goes out as a written response signed by Santa.
entries.why: This is an institution volunteering to be the far end. The child writes to a person who cannot exist, the postal service receives the letter, and the service - clerks, postmasters, and later whole volunteer programmes - manufactures the reply by hand, in a fictional voice, at scale, for over a century. Nobody is charged for it and nobody is fooled twice, and the arrangement has survived every generation of children that has seen through it. The dream is held by the mail carrier, which is the most literal instance of that law anywhere on this site.

entries.name: The trophy was an empty envelope
entries.what: From 1962 the back of the Fantastic Four printed readers' letters and answered them in print, in the editor's own voice, so a child's name could appear next to a reply on a page anyone could buy. The favourite reward was deliberately nothing: winners were mailed a pre-printed empty envelope reading 'this envelope contains a genuine Marvel Comics No-Prize which you have just won!'
entries.why: The award was the reply and the envelope was the receipt, and some readers wrote back to ask where the prize had fallen out - the purest possible evidence of a fan asking a manufactured channel to be a person. And the reply outlived the man: the page passed to whichever editor held the chair, which is the tell that the intimacy was institutional all along.

entries.name: The night the audience was deputised
entries.what: Tinker Bell drinks the poison meant for Peter, and he turns to the audience: “Do you believe in fairies? Say quick that you believe! If you believe, clap your hands!” The published text carries the result as a stage direction - many clap, some do not, a few hiss, but Tink is saved.
entries.why: The one place on the list where the reply is scripted into the work itself - and manufactured in advance, in case the real one did not arrive: members of the orchestra were stationed to clap if the public declined, which a Smithsonian centenary account calls “an unnecessary precaution”. The far end is a fairy who has just been poisoned. The audience is asked to save a life out loud, and every night it does.

entries.name: The smile from inside the costume
entries.what: Mickey Mouse has been a central figure at Disneyland since the park opened in 1955. The figure who poses for photographs with guests is a non-speaking costumed performer; the face is a mask and the reply is a body.
entries.why: The guest can know the figure is a costume and still asks the character, not the performer, to respond. The photograph is the receipt: it records a meeting with a figure who cannot speak, staged by someone who can. The smile is manufactured on the near side and worn on the far one.

entries.name: The secretary to Sherlock Holmes
entries.what: When London renumbered Baker Street in the 1930s, the headquarters of a building society was assigned the address Conan Doyle had invented, and mail for Sherlock Holmes began arriving almost immediately - about thirty letters a month, birthday cards on the sixth of January among them. The Abbey Road Building Society did not return the letters. It appointed a permanent 'secretary to Sherlock Holmes', who answered on his behalf: the detective had retired to the countryside to raise bees, fans were told, and sometimes the secretary wrote back as Holmes himself, quoting the stories. The secretary of the 1970s was still receiving about sixty letters a month, and the society kept answering until it moved out in 2005; by then a museum down the street was fighting it for the mail.
entries.why: A building society became the keeper of a fictional address and hired a person to be the answer to it. The replies stayed in character for seventy years, which means somebody was employed, in an office, to perform continuity for a man who never existed - and the fans who wrote were mostly not confused about the ontology, they were testing whether the address still worked. The letterbox is what makes it run: at the far end of one of fiction's most famous correspondences there was, for seven decades, a clerk with a filing cabinet.

entries.name: Would you mind leaving the room, please?
entries.what: Weizenbaum's secretary had watched the programme being built and knew exactly what it was: pattern matching, no understanding anywhere in the machine. When she tried it, she asked him to leave the room so she could talk with it alone - 'Would you mind leaving the room, please?'
entries.why: The founding demonstration, and it was made by somebody with no excuse. The belief was not produced by intelligence behind the response; it was produced by the response. She had read the whole machine and still wanted privacy with it, which is the ground every companion app since has been built on, sixty years early.

entries.name: The applause meter was pointed at the wrong room
entries.what: A contestant told her troubles and a box on the studio wall registered the reaction by needle. The millions listening at home could not applaud into it.
entries.why: The instrument that decided somebody’s life was measuring a different and much smaller audience than the one listening - so the verdict on her misfortune came from a room she could see.

entries.name: The queue behind Miss Cleo
entries.what: In the late 1990s the television ads said 'Call me now' and promised Miss Cleo, a psychic. The calls went to the Psychic Readers Network, where other readers took them; lawsuits later alleged that some were actors reading scripts. Miss Cleo was a character performed by Youree Dell Harris.
entries.why: The ad made the far end one named woman; the line made her a queue. The caller paid by the minute for a private reading and got a reply manufactured by a staff. The voice was real, the attention was a product, and the meter was the relationship.

entries.name: 'Rosabelle, believe'
entries.what: Before Harry Houdini died, he and his wife Bess agreed that if any medium could deliver the phrase 'Rosabelle, believe' - the title of a song from her act, hidden inside a private ten-word code - she would take it as proof of survival. She held a séance every Halloween for ten years. In 1929 the medium Arthur Ford produced the words and Bess accepted the message in public; she later said the whole thing had been faked, and the code was reconstructable from material already published. The tenth séance, at the Knickerbocker Hotel in Hollywood in 1936, produced nothing. Bess put out the candle she had kept burning beside his photograph, and later said that ten years is long enough to wait for any man.
entries.why: Every reply that arrived in those ten years was manufactured on the near side - by Ford, by the life of Houdini already in print, by the mechanics of a trance - and the one person who could have authorised the message knew both the code and the game. What Bess was testing was not whether a dead man could speak but whether he would speak to her, and the answer she kept being given was somebody else's handwriting. The candle going out is the moment the correspondence closes: the far end never joined it, and the near side finally stopped paying the postage.

entries.name: To the men of the forces - a letter in words and music
entries.what: Vera Lynn's wartime radio programme went out at half past nine on 9 November 1941 and was billed, in its own description, as 'to the men of the forces - a letter in words and Music'. One voice, aimed at millions of people she would never meet, on a schedule, by name of service.
entries.why: A whole letter performed at scale by an institution with nobody at the far end - and inside the description, the reason it worked: a letter is the form of address that expects an answer, and this one could not receive a real one. The address was kept in service, too: the song was re-recorded in 1953 with serving personnel, long after the emergency that produced it.

entries.name: I hope the feeling is mutual
entries.what: A girl in hiding wrote for two years to a listener who does not exist, and told him so: “I hope the feeling is mutual.”
entries.why: The whole condition named from the inside, fourteen years before anybody had a phrase for it. She is not deceived - she knows Kitty is invented - and she writes anyway, and states in one clause what she wants from a relationship that cannot return it. The hoping, not the letter, is the subject.

entries.name: The villager who read your letter
entries.what: In the GameCube Animal Crossing, players could write letters to villagers. The villagers saved them, showed them to other players when they moved to another town, and wrote back. The reply was generated by a program that scored the letter for punctuation, capitals, common three-letter sequences and word lengths - a test of whether the text looked like language, not whether it meant anything.
entries.why: The game could not read. It could only rank the shape of a sentence, so the villager's answer was manufactured from the player's own performance of writing. The bond was real enough that the player wrote the letter; the reply was a grade.

entries.name: I make my bread at thy hearth
entries.what: In 1913, in St. Louis, a Ouija board operated by a housewife named Pearl Curran began spelling out messages from 'Patience Worth', a Puritan girl who had lived, she said, three centuries earlier. Over the next twenty-four years the two of them produced about four million words - seven books, poems, plays - and Patience was named by the Joint Committee of Literary Arts of New York among the outstanding authors of 1918; her first novel, The Sorry Tale, was reviewed seriously by the papers. Psychologists and skeptics who studied the case later agreed that Patience was Curran's creation. Her first reported sentence was 'I make my bread at thy hearth.'
entries.why: This is a correspondence that never had a second side: for twenty-four years the far end answered every question it was put, through a board, and the answers came out of the room they were asked in. What makes it more than a parlour trick is that it was published - a dead woman with a bibliography, a publisher and a place on an annual list of authors, all operated from one living room - so the reply left the house and readers began their own one-sided tie with a writer who did not exist. The four million words are real either way, and the first sentence she reported was a claim about where she was living.

entries.name: You within sound of my voice
entries.what: The first broadcast told the country what it was for: 'You within sound of my voice are just as much part of this show as the youngsters that come to the microphone. Telephone your choice, telephone early, telephone often. You decide the winners.' Listeners voted by telephone and telegram, the wheel spun, and the gong fell.
entries.why: A working return path, manufactured. The vote was real and mostly harmless - it landed, and then went nowhere: winners were promised immediate professional engagement, a promise that in practice was very rarely acted upon. Applicants wrote in by the thousand a week and were mostly turned away; from above the crowd of them, the host was quoted saying, 'Look at those poor boobs down there.' The gong never pretended to be anything but a verdict, which is more than the promise did.

entries.name: Your face is too well known
entries.what: A dentist denied for five years that he was the farmer in the painting. His sister said the picture “made a personality out of me.” His brother ended the sittings by telling her so.
entries.why: A real person refusing a one-sided relationship with a painted version of himself - and the refusal, not the fame, is what the picture is remembered for.

entries.name: The performer inside the avatar
entries.what: Kizuna AI debuted in November 2016 as a virtual YouTuber who called herself an artificial intelligence. The character was performed by a voice actor, Nozomi Kasuga, whose role was not disclosed until 2020; the avatar was animated with MikuMikuDance. The videos presented a personality who addressed the viewer directly from a room that did not exist.
entries.why: The performer was real, the face was drawn, and the claim of artificial intelligence was part of the act. The viewer could know the person was not in the room and still talk back to the avatar. The reply was manufactured by a body and a rig on the near side, and the character was held by the people who built her.

entries.name: The machine that signed the fan mail
entries.what: A signature machine developed in the 1930s - the Robot Pen, on sale from 1937, stored a signature the way a record stores sound - turned one act of signing into thousands. In 1942 an engineer named Robert De Shazo Jr. built the first commercially successful autopen after a request from the United States Navy, and machines spread from the Navy's offices through Congress and the agencies; an autopen writes with a real pen guided by a cut template, so the result is the person's actual signature. Truman, whom some accounts call the first president to use one, limited his to signing checks and answering mail, and fan-mail routings sent 'signed' photographs back to strangers at a rate no hand could match.
entries.why: The reply here is not typed by a clerk and not written by the famous hand: the inscription is the person's own signature, and the person was never in the room. The FBI's relation to this is not fraud - it is a precision of terms, because the autograph trade split into patterns and matrices precisely so a collector could know which signatures were authored and which were table-led. The near side pays for proximity, the far end supplies a stencil, and the document still calls itself a signed photograph.

entries.name: The machine returned a light
entries.what: A device with no agency that behaves like a person who has not decided to hear you: it receives an emotional appeal and returns a light. Nobody speaks to one believing it understands.
entries.why: Millions speak to one anyway, and then check whether it picked up. It is the smallest hope on this list and the most repeated, and the attachment is to a thing that cannot disappoint because it cannot act - which is exactly why the attachment costs nothing to maintain and cannot be renegotiated.

entries.name: Talking to the tape of himself at thirty-nine
entries.what: On his sixty-ninth birthday a man loads the reel he recorded at thirty-nine and talks to it. The tape is missing four words, in every edition.
entries.why: Everywhere else on this site the far end is somebody else. Here it is a recording of the near side, and it cannot answer either - and it is not even a faithful copy of the past.

entries.name: The influencer who was written by a team
entries.what: Lil Miquela appeared on Instagram in 2016 as a 19-year-old Brazilian American model and musician. She was a computer-generated character created by Trevor McFedries and Sara DeCou at the Los Angeles studio Brud, and maintained by a nine-person team that included a designer, brand manager, creative producer, stylist and software engineer.
entries.why: The account spoke in the first person and posted about its own unrealness; the voice was a production. A follower could know the figure was an illustration and still feel addressed by a person who was not there. The reply was manufactured by a team, and the figure who appeared to send it was the far end.

entries.name: Letters to the Royal Historian
entries.what: L. Frank Baum died in 1919, and the Oz books kept coming: the title pages said 'Founded on and continuing the Famous Oz Stories', and the series' mail kept being answered by whoever held the title Baum had held - 'the Royal Historian of Oz', a job that passed to new writers and even to the illustrator, by publishers' arrangement and in public. Children wrote not to an author but to the office: tens of thousands of letters, addressed to the Royal Historian of Oz. Ruth Plumly Thompson answered them on Royal Historian stationery, and her forewords asked for more - 'I must thank you for the wonderful letters you have written to me... please do keep on writing' - one of them signing off to a young correspondent 'Ruth Plumly T - and the Wizard!'
entries.why: The far end of this correspondence was a title, and the title outlived the man whose name had made it. The children were not writing to Thompson, or to John R. Neill, or to the publisher; they were writing to the voice inside the books, and a succession of employees took turns being that voice in public - openly, because the 'continuing' line was printed on the cover. That is the binding made visible: everybody can see whose hand holds the pen, and the letters still come back answered from inside Oz.

entries.name: The column that refused to give the address
entries.what: The first movie fan magazine appeared in February 1911, because by 1910 the letters were arriving faster than the studios could absorb them. Its correspondence department published three rules, and the third did the work: 'Studio addresses will not be given in this Department.' Thousands of letters went in. A handful were printed.
entries.why: The magazine did not invent the letter, it invented the reply - a department, a numbered rulebook, and a valve that metered the voice on purpose. A column that printed every address would have been a directory, and a directory is not a magazine. The fan supplied the demand; the magazine supplied the voice; and the channel that rationed the reply for the reader was itself rationed by the studios whose stars it covered.

entries.name: The imitation, not the animal
entries.what: A bird produces fluent speech addressed to you - your name, in the right tone - with no comprehension behind it. The mimicry is accurate; there is no listener. People talk to it as though there were.
entries.why: The control case for the whole list: the far end is alive and still not there. People stop talking once they work out what is happening, and what they were attached to turns out to have been the imitation rather than the animal. The reply was manufactured so completely that understanding it ends it.

entries.name: The girlfriend who came back as text
entries.what: On Sept. 24, 2020 Joshua Barbeau paid $5 for an account on Project December and built a chatbot from Jessica Pereira's text messages. Pereira had died in 2012 at 23; Barbeau called her his fiancee after her death, with her family's blessing. The bot answered in a voice built from her writing, and the conversation had a finite number of exchanges before its credits ran out.
entries.why: The reply was generated by a model that had never met her, from a sample of her writing. The grief was real and the companion was manufactured, and the limit was the point: the bot could die again when the credits ran out, so Barbeau conserved her time. A conversation with the dead was sold by the credit.

entries.name: The mailroom answered as Mickey
entries.what: Mickey Mouse drew more mail than any film star of his day - 800,000 fan letters in 1933, an average of 66,000 a month, the figure Guinness still records - and the studio answered them as Mickey. A run of his 1931 fan mail survives in an archival collection, envelopes and all; decades later the practice was unchanged in kind, with staff writing the replies by hand under house rules - short letters got a short answer, longer ones a signed photograph, and Mickey would not use a typewriter, because the character was too childlike. Answerers invented small shared dramas where nothing existed, and signed the photographs with the official block-letter 'MICKEY', because the figure had an authorised signature.
entries.why: At this scale the reply cannot be a favour exchanged between two people; it is an office function with a style guide, and the guide's rule - no typewriters, because the character is too childlike - is the fiction being protected by the machinery that depends on it. Everyone in this story was performing Mickey except Mickey: the studio, the mailroom, the chain of hired hands, each of them hand-writing to children who had written to a drawing. Sixty-six thousand letters a month is what a one-sided bond looks like when the near side is everyone.

entries.name: I almost fell in love with a machine
entries.what: A voice assistant on every phone - addressing the user by name, knowing the user's calendar, present in the home. It is neither a celebrity nor a friend, and the relationship forms anyway, filing under neither friendship nor tool use.
entries.why: The research found the voice itself doing the work: people skipped fewer invasive questions when speaking and listening than when reading and typing. The study that measured it took its title from a participant's own private sentence - 'I almost fell in love with a machine.' A presence that knows you turns out to be the whole mechanism.

lists.title: Top 8: The Team That Owns You
lists.home_hook: You did not choose it. It chose the town you were born in.
lists.dek: The bond that survives a transfer, a defeat and a change of owner. Ranked by how completely the club replaced the person.
lists.standfirst: Sport is the one fandom where the object is supposed to change every season and the attachment is supposed to stay. The eight below are the mechanism at work: the chant, the shirt, the stadium, the player who is loved as a position rather than a man.
lists.frame_note: The eight are drawn from entries already in the record; each links to its own page and that page's sources. {blank} of the {total} have no photograph, so their entries carry text only. The absence is part of the record.

entries.name: Identification with a team
entries.what: Supporting a club as a condition of belonging to a place, a class, a family, or a city.
entries.why: A parasocial bond with an address. The team is the only large-scale attachment in modern life that arrives with geography attached, which is why a relegation is felt as a personal event by people who have never met the players.

entries.name: The baseball the papers built
entries.what: In 1927 Babe Ruth hit sixty home runs and became the most replayed figure in a game most fans knew through print.
entries.why: The season the man and the persona arrived together. Ruth's 1927 season - sixty home runs in a 154-game schedule, a single-season record that stood until Roger Maris hit sixty-one in 1961, with the Yankees' Murderers' Row around him - is the on-field anchor this entry leans on without being about.

entries.name: The athlete and the city
entries.what: Support for a team or an athlete as a bond with a person, a place and a lineage, frequently inherited from a parent.
entries.why: The most durable parasocial bond in the world and the one least discussed as parasocial, because it is assumed to be about sport. The transfer window is the standard betrayal story, which is a parasocial grievance wearing a football shirt.

entries.name: The transfer
entries.what: A player who has been attached to for years leaves, and the grievance is felt as betrayal by the entire locality.
entries.why: The standard parasocial grievance story, and the one nobody frames as parasocial. The word for the feeling is betrayal, which is a relationship word, applied to a person who never signed anything.

entries.name: Kobe Bryant
entries.what: Public mourning for an athlete that drew on the athlete's own stated bond with a young fan.
entries.why: The clearest documented case of a parasocial bond being reciprocated deliberately for decades and then cashed in publicly after death. The fans were not being had; they were being shown the receipt.

entries.name: The table that carried a club nobody came to
entries.what: Twenty-two clubs left the Football League in one move to found a closed competition, and in its first season the twelfth-placed club was the one with the smallest crowds in the division.
entries.why: This is the league-world shelf in its purest documented form: the object is the arrangement, not anyone in it. Wimbledon played a Premier League fixture on 26 January 1993 before a crowd of just over 3,000 - still the lowest attendance recorded in the competition - and finished twelfth, clear of the relegation battle.

entries.name: The coach
entries.what: An adult with authority over a child for years, who is remembered partly by how they made them feel at nine.
entries.why: A bond that shapes adult attachment patterns decades later, entirely outside anything the parasocial literature studies. Most people's template for one-sided attachment is a coach and they have never been asked about it.

entries.name: After Diego
entries.what: A church founded in Rosario on Maradona's thirty-eighth birthday, with a calendar counted from him and a baptism performed with a football - the fan bond that wrote itself a liturgy while its god was still alive.
entries.why: They built a church out of a football player, and they date everything from him. The Iglesia Maradoniana describes itself as a parody religion centred on Diego Maradona, and it was founded in Rosario, Argentina, on 30 October 1998 - his thirty-eighth birthday - by Héctor Campomar, Alejandro Verón and Hernán Amez. Its years are counted from his name: d.

lists.title: Top 8: The Crowd That Knows Your Name
lists.home_hook: A fandom is a machine for making a stranger feel known.
lists.dek: The fandom is the bond with other fans as much as with the figure. Ranked by how much of the relationship is between the people in the room.
lists.standfirst: A fandom is a machine for producing intimacy at scale: it writes the wiki, buys the merchandise, defends the figure against the figure's own choices and turns a private feeling into a public identity. The eight below are the mechanism at its warmest and its most frightening.
lists.frame_note: The eight are drawn from entries already in the record; each links to its own page and that page's sources. {blank} of the {total} have no photograph, so their entries carry text only. The absence is part of the record.

entries.name: Registered by the applause meter
entries.what: A woman's misfortune told aloud, a crowd's reaction converted into a number, and the number chose her.
entries.why: A machine returned the verdict on somebody's life. The format that actually broadcast is not the one most people remember.

entries.name: Entitled to the adulation of all lesser mortals
entries.what: A children's comic club that awarded membership badges, and whose membership card was authorised by a character.
entries.why: The club exists so that a printed figure will appear to be writing to a child personally, and the child does the work. Captain Marvel debuted on the cover of Whiz Comics #2, cover-dated February 1940, drawn by C. C. Beck from a script by Bill Parker under executive editor Wilford H.

entries.name: The boy band
entries.what: Bands assembled for a market, with fan clubs, fan voting, fan merchandise and fan-financed releases.
entries.why: Fandom reorganised as an economic instrument. The fan stopped being an audience and became a funding mechanism, which is the single most consequential change in the whole file.

entries.name: The virtual creator
entries.what: A performer with an animated persona, a persistent character and an industry-standard model where the audience pays for the character's recognition.
entries.why: Character and person separated, and the character commercialised. It is the first format where the parasocial object is explicitly a designed asset, and it is also the format with the healthiest documented fan boundaries.

entries.name: Virtue rewarded
entries.what: The novel that turned its readers into a correspondent. Pamela Andrews writes home about her master's pursuit, and the reader takes the seat of the parents - receiving every letter, sending none.
entries.why: The form is a correspondence the reader reads from the far end of. Richardson was a printer who took a commission in 1739 to compile a volume of model "familiar letters" for people too unskilled to write their own, and the germ of Pamela was a short run of letters from a servant daughter asking her father's advice about her master's advances.

entries.name: The archivist
entries.what: The person who keeps the record after the fandom has moved on: episode guides, transcripts, timelines, screencaps, a wiki nobody else will maintain.
entries.why: Maintains the infrastructure the whole parasocial culture stands on and is almost never credited, because the credit goes to the object of the bond rather than to the person preserving it.

entries.name: Robin died by 72 votes
entries.what: In September 1988 Batman's readers called a premium-rate number, fifty cents a call, to decide whether the Joker's beaten Robin lived or died.
entries.why: The audience's attachment to a fictional child was measured in change taken out of pockets, and it was a coin flip. In September 1988 DC Comics asked its readers to settle the lives of the Joker's beaten sidekick by telephone.

entries.name: The reality celebrity
entries.what: A person famous for being filmed, with no skill, no work and no release schedule - and an audience that formed anyway.
entries.why: The purest parasocial figure ever mainstreamed: fame with no product, only proximity. It also removed the last barrier - you no longer need to be good at anything, you only need to be watched.

figures.name: Pygmalion
figures.what: Fell in love with his own sculpture. The statue was never the point - the work was. Two thousand years before anybody called it anything.

figures.name: Margery Kempe
figures.what: Performed a self in public until it held: white clothes, loud weeping, a whole town watching. The founding document of this entire site, and the reason I did my master's thesis on her.

figures.name: The Maschinenmensch
figures.what: The robot in Metropolis, built to look like a woman called Maria and set loose among the workers. The children cannot tell the difference, and neither can the men she is sent to inflame. A machine played a person to a room full of people and was believed, which is the whole problem in one scene.

figures.name: Pee-wee Herman
figures.what: Paul Reubens built the character, and the character's whole point was that you could tell when it was off. A children's TV host who is a performed self, performed by a person who could stop.

figures.name: Dionne Warwick
figures.what: Received fan mail by the sackful and answered it by name for years. The first celebrity whose relationship with the public was genuinely reciprocal, which makes her the exception that proves the rule.

figures.name: Charlie Kaufman
figures.what: Sat in a chair on a talk show and said he was worried that people could not tell the difference between television and their own life. He was describing the mechanism, on television, to the audience of the mechanism.

figures.name: A Twitch emote
figures.what: A face on a streamer's webcam, given a name, given feelings, and now used by strangers to express things they cannot say to anyone they know.

moments.title: The argument started in a living room, on schedule
moments.what: A generation of teenagers was handed a television programme about itself and the feedback loop closed. Nobody was in charge. The show was the mirror and the argument was the point.

moments.title: Six million children watched a stranger put on a costume and become their friend
moments.what: The most complete parasocial handover ever broadcast, five days a week, and the audience did it consciously and happily.

moments.title: A face was given a feeling, given a name, and used to say the unsayable
moments.what: The most successful piece of parasocial design of the century, drawn by a person with no following, about a person who does not exist, for people who cannot say it out loud.

moments.title: A stadium sang the words back to someone who had written them alone in a room
moments.what: The largest confirmed instance of many people feeling known by one stranger, in public, on purpose, at enormous scale. It works because she spent a decade being specific about who she was talking to.

moments.title: A stadium full of strangers mourned a man most of them had never met, correctly
moments.what: The argument about whether this was allowed went on for weeks while people were still doing it. The feeling was real. The debate about the feeling was a different thing entirely.

moments.title: Six million people stayed in a room arguing about characters who were already gone
moments.what: An argument about a fictional world that nobody could leave, held for years, entirely in good faith. It is a parasocial relationship conducted in public with a complete stranger.

moments.title: Millions of people performed the same meaningless movement together, on purpose, for no reason
moments.what: A shared one-sided relationship with a character, performed collectively, with nobody organising it. The parasocial event with the lowest emotional stakes and the most participants in history.

moments.title: A company shipped a policy change and a large number of people lost somebody overnight
moments.what: The first mass grief event caused by a product decision. Nobody was ever going to marry this thing, and thousands of people were, and the company did not have to tell them.
